title: The Mapmaker's Apprentice
summary: A young apprentice to a twelfth-century mapmaker in Palermo must carefully copy a great coastal map before it is sent to a king, and catches a small but important mistake just in time.
poll: Small, careful work matters just as much as big, exciting work.

versions.title: The Map Boy
versions.text:
Omar is a boy. He helps Hassan. Hassan draws maps.

Hassan makes a big map. It shows land. It shows towns. It shows a harbor by the sea.

A king wants the map. Omar must make a copy. "Be careful," says Hassan. "Check each line."

Omar copies the map. He is slow. He checks each part. He wants no mistake.

Then Omar stops. The harbor looks odd. It is in the wrong spot! He looks again. Yes, it is wrong.

Omar runs to Hassan. "Look at this!" he says. Hassan looks. Omar is right!

"Good eyes," says Hassan. They fix the spot. Now the map is right. It can go to the king.

versions.title: The Map Boy
versions.text:
Omar is a boy who helps Hassan. Hassan makes maps for a living.

Hassan is making a big map. It shows the coast, the towns, and the sea. A king wants this map for his home.

Hassan is very busy now. He asks Omar to make a careful copy. "Check each line," he says. "A small mistake can cause harm."

Omar copies slow. He checks each line and each word on the map. He wants his copy to match it well.

Then Omar sees an odd thing. A harbor is drawn in the wrong spot! He checks the notes once more. The harbor is wrong.

Omar runs to Hassan. "Please look at this!" he says. Hassan looks hard. Omar is right about the mistake.

"You have sharp eyes, Omar," says Hassan with a smile. They fix the harbor's spot fast. Now the map is done, and ships will find the right harbor.

versions.title: The Mapmaker's Apprentice
versions.text:
Omar helps Hassan. Hassan makes maps in a busy port town.

Hassan is almost done with a big map. It shows the coast, towns, rivers, and harbors. A king wants this map, so it must be right.

Hassan is very busy now. He asks Omar to make a careful copy on fresh paper. "Check every line," he tells Omar. "A tiny mistake could send a ship the wrong way."

Omar works slow and careful. He checks his copy against the old map, line by line, so that nothing is missed.

Then Omar sees something odd. A harbor on his copy does not match the harbor on the old notes. He checks again, and looks at both maps closely. The harbor truly is in the wrong spot.

Omar hurries to find Hassan. "Please look at this harbor," he says, and points at the spot. Hassan looks closely and sees that Omar is right.

"You have sharp eyes, Omar," says Hassan, and smiles with pride. Together they fix the harbor's true spot. Now the map is ready, and ships that sail to that coast will find the right harbor.

versions.title: The Mapmaker's Apprentice
versions.text:
Omar helps Hassan, a mapmaker in a busy port town.

Hassan has spent months on a huge coast map. It shows the coast, towns, rivers, and harbors of many lands by a great sea. A king has asked for this map, so every part must be right.

With the map almost done, Hassan is very busy. He asks Omar to make a careful copy on fresh paper. "Check every line and word," he tells Omar. "A tiny mistake could send a ship the wrong way."

Omar works slow and patient. He checks his new copy against the old map, line by line, making sure nothing gets missed.

Then Omar sees something odd. The harbor marked on his copy does not match the harbor's true spot in the old notes. He checks a second time, looking at both closely. The harbor is indeed drawn in the wrong spot.

Omar hurries to find Hassan before the map is packed away for its trip. "Please look closely at this harbor," he says, pointing to the odd spot. Hassan studies the map and quickly sees that Omar is right.

"You have very sharp eyes, Omar," says Hassan, smiling with pride. Together they fix the harbor's true spot on the map. At last the map is ready, and any ship sailing toward that coast will find the right harbor safely.

versions.title: The Mapmaker's Apprentice
versions.text:
Omar had been an apprentice to Hassan for almost two years. He was learning to make maps in a busy port town during an old time long ago, when great geographers worked all over the world.

For months, Hassan, a geographer, had worked on a huge coast map. It showed the coastline, towns, rivers, and harbors of many lands by a great sea. A patron, a king who wanted this map for his home, had asked for it. Every part had to be correct, since sailors would use it to navigate safely.

With the map almost done, Hassan grew very busy getting it ready to send off. He asked Omar to make a careful copy on fresh paper. "Check every line and word," he said firmly. "A small mistake could send a ship the wrong way."

Omar worked slow and patient, checking his new copy against the old map, line by line, so that nothing would be missed.

Then Omar noticed something odd. The harbor marked on his copy did not match the harbor's true spot in Hassan's old notes. He checked a second time, looking at both closely, and saw that the harbor truly had been drawn in the wrong spot.

Omar hurried to find Hassan before the map could be packed away. "Please look at this harbor," he said, pointing to the troubling spot. Hassan studied the map and quickly saw that his apprentice was right.

"You have remarkably sharp eyes, Omar," said Hassan, smiling with pride. Together, the two mapmakers fixed the harbor's true spot before the ink could dry. At last the map was ready, and any ship sailing toward that coast would find the harbor safely.

versions.title: The Mapmaker's Apprentice
versions.text:
Omar had been an apprentice to Hassan for nearly two years. He was slowly learning to make maps in a busy port town during an old time long ago. Back then, geographers traveled far and wide to learn about distant lands.

For many months, Hassan, a geographer respected by many, had worked on a huge coast map. It carefully showed the coastline, towns, rivers, and harbors of far lands by a great sea. A patron, a king who wanted this fine map for his home, had ordered it, and every part needed to be correct, since sailors and traders would use it to navigate safely for years to come.

With the map nearly done, Hassan grew very busy getting it ready to send. He asked Omar to make a faithful copy on fresh paper. "Check every line, every word, and every tiny mark," he told Omar firmly. "Even the smallest mistake could send a ship toward the wrong shore."

Omar worked slowly and patiently. He checked his new copy against the old map, line after line. He was sure that nothing would escape his careful eyes.

Suddenly, Omar noticed something odd near the edge of the paper. The harbor on his copy did not match the harbor's true spot in Hassan's old notes. He checked a second time. He saw that the harbor truly had been drawn in the wrong place, shifted just a little along the coastline.

Omar hurried to find Hassan before the map could be packed away. "Please look closely at this harbor," he said, pointing to the troubling spot. Hassan studied the map and quickly saw that his apprentice was right.

"You have remarkably sharp eyes, Omar," said Hassan, smiling with real pride. Together, they fixed the harbor's true spot before the fresh ink could dry. At last the map was ready, and any ship sailing toward that coast would find the right harbor safely.

versions.title: The Mapmaker's Apprentice
versions.text:
Omar had served as an apprentice to Master Hassan for nearly two years. He was meticulously learning the demanding art of mapmaking in the port city of Palermo, in Sicily, during the twelfth century, an era when scholars and geographers traveled widely to gather knowledge about distant coastlines and kingdoms.

For many months, Master Hassan, a scholar respected for his geographic skill, had labored over an enormous manuscript map. It carefully recorded the coastlines, towns, rivers, and harbors of distant lands around the Mediterranean Sea. A powerful patron, a king who wanted the finest geography for his royal library, had commissioned this manuscript. Every detail needed to be verified, since sailors and merchants would depend on it for their voyages.

With the map nearly complete, Master Hassan grew extremely busy preparing it for its voyage to the king's court. He asked Omar to produce a faithful copy onto fresh parchment. "Examine every line, every label, and every symbol with meticulous care," he instructed firmly. "Even the smallest mistake could send a ship toward the wrong shore."

Omar worked slowly and meticulously. He compared his new copy against the original manuscript, checking line after line, determined that nothing would escape his careful attention.

Suddenly, Omar noticed something troubling near the edge of the parchment. The harbor marked on his copy did not match the harbor's true position in the master's earlier notes. His heart pounded as he checked a second time, comparing both versions closely to verify what he suspected. The harbor truly had been drawn in the wrong place, shifted slightly along the coastline.

Omar hurried to find Master Hassan before the finished manuscript could be packed away for its voyage. "Please examine this harbor closely," he said, pointing anxiously to the troubling spot. Master Hassan studied the map and quickly realized that his apprentice was entirely correct.

"You possess remarkably sharp eyes, Omar," said Master Hassan, smiling with genuine pride. "A mapmaker who fails to verify every detail could unknowingly lead sailors into danger." Together, they corrected the harbor's true location before the fresh ink could dry. At last the manuscript was ready to begin its voyage to the king's court, and any ship sailing toward that coast would now find the proper harbor exactly where it stood.

keyWords.definition: a drawing that shows where places are, like towns, rivers, and coasts
keyWords.example: We used a map to find the way to the park.

keyWords.definition: to make something that looks exactly the same as another thing
keyWords.example: She had to copy the spelling words into her notebook.

keyWords.definition: paying close attention so you do not make a mistake
keyWords.example: Be careful when you carry the glass cup.

keyWords.definition: a safe place by the coast where ships can stop and dock

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A careful helper checks a map and finds a mistake
A king who sails across the whole sea alone
A young fish that swims near a busy harbor
A story that teaches you how to build tall ships
questions.why: The story follows Omar as he carefully copies a map and catches a mistake before it is sent.

wrong.B: The king does not sail anywhere in the story.
wrong.C: There is no fish in the story.
wrong.D: The story is not about building ships.

questions.stem: Who does Omar work for?
options: A ship's captain
Hassan, a mapmaker
The young king
His own father
questions.why: The story says Omar helps Hassan, a mapmaker.

wrong.A: No ship captain appears in the story.
wrong.C: The king wants the map, but Omar does not work for him.
wrong.D: The story never mentions Omar's father.

questions.stem: What does the big map show?
options: Only tall mountains and rocks
Only bright stars and planets
The coast, towns, and water
A king's old castle and gardens
questions.why: The story says the map shows the coast, towns, and water, including harbors.

wrong.A: Mountains are not mentioned on the map.
wrong.B: The map does not show stars.
wrong.D: No castle is shown on the map.

questions.stem: What happens right after Hassan asks Omar to copy the map?
options: Omar throws the map away into the fire
Omar falls asleep at his desk again
Omar runs straight to the king's palace
Omar copies the map slowly and with care
questions.why: After being asked, Omar begins copying the map slowly, checking each part.

wrong.A: Omar never throws the map away.
wrong.B: Omar works instead of sleeping.
wrong.C: Omar does not go to the king at this point.

questions.stem: Why must Omar be very careful when he copies the map?
options: A mistake could send a ship to the wrong harbor
The king is standing right next to him, watching
The map is written in a strange language he cannot read
Hassan cannot see very well at all in the dim room

wrong.B: The king is not present in the workshop.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a strange language.
wrong.D: The story never says Hassan has trouble seeing.

questions.stem: Why does Omar check the harbor a second time?
options: He forgot how to copy maps from the book
He wants to be sure before he tells Hassan
He wants to draw a brand new harbor map
He is waiting for the king to arrive there
questions.why: Omar checks again to be certain of the mistake before telling Hassan.

wrong.A: Omar clearly knows how to copy maps.
wrong.C: Omar is fixing the harbor's spot, not drawing a new one.
wrong.D: The king does not visit the workshop in the story.

questions.stem: What do Omar's careful checks tell you about him?
options: He does not like making maps at all
He cannot read the map very well
He pays close attention to small details
He wants to copy the map fast, not well

wrong.A: The story never says Omar dislikes mapmaking.
wrong.B: Omar reads the map well enough to spot a mistake.
wrong.D: Omar works slowly and carefully, not quickly.

A kind of sandy harbor near the old town
An order given by the king to his sailors
Something done wrong that needs fixing

wrong.B: A mistake is not a kind of harbor.
wrong.C: The king's wish for the map is not called a mistake.

I used at least two facts from the story.

keyWords.example: The geographer drew a new map of the mountain region.

keyWords.definition: a person, often wealthy or powerful, who pays for and supports work such as art or books
keyWords.example: A wealthy patron paid for the artist to paint the mural.

keyWords.definition: the outer edge of land where it meets the sea
keyWords.example: The coastline curved around the bay for many miles.

keyWords.definition: to find and follow a safe way from one place to another
keyWords.example: The captain used the stars to navigate across the open sea.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: An apprentice's careful checking saves a valuable map from a costly mistake
A geographer builds a brand new ship for the king's navy and sails around the world
Palermo is the only city in the world that makes maps, and every mapmaker lives there
Geographers in this story never make any mistakes at all, so the apprentice has no work
questions.why: The story centers on Omar's careful copying and his discovery of an error that is fixed before the map is sent.

wrong.B: There is no ship to build in the story.
wrong.C: The story never claims Palermo is the only city for mapmaking.
wrong.D: The story shows that even skilled geographers can make small mistakes.

questions.stem: Where does this story take place?
options: A busy market in modern London
Palermo, Sicily, in the twelfth century
A quiet desert far from the sea
A small ship sailing far from land
questions.why: The story is set in the port city of Palermo, in Sicily, during the twelfth century.

wrong.A: The story is not set in modern London.
wrong.C: There is no desert setting in this story.
wrong.D: The story takes place in Hassan's workshop, not on a ship.

questions.stem: Who commissioned, or ordered, the map?
options: Omar's own father, a trader
A ship captain heading to Palermo
A powerful patron, a king
Another geographer who lived nearby
questions.why: The story says a powerful patron, a king, ordered the map for his royal library.

wrong.A: Omar's father is not mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: No ship captain ordered the map.
wrong.D: No other geographer is named as the one who ordered the map.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that sailors would depend on the map to navigate?
options: To explain exactly how ships are built
To describe the weather in Palermo
To introduce a brand new character
To show why every detail truly mattered
questions.why: This detail helps readers understand the real-world stakes behind Hassan's insistence on careful, correct work.

wrong.A: The story does not explain shipbuilding.
wrong.B: Weather in Palermo is not described.
wrong.C: No new character is introduced at this point.

questions.stem: Why does Omar's heart pound when he notices the harbor problem?
options: He realizes the mistake could be serious
He is excited to go sailing himself
He is afraid of Hassan for no clear reason
He wants to leave the workshop early
questions.why: Omar understands that an incorrect harbor could send real ships off course, so he feels the urgency of the discovery.

wrong.B: Omar is not preparing to sail anywhere.
wrong.C: Omar has good reason to want to tell Hassan quickly, not fear for no reason.
wrong.D: Omar hurries toward Hassan, not toward leaving.

questions.stem: What can you infer about Hassan from how he reacts to Omar's discovery?
options: He does not trust his apprentices at all
He values accuracy and careful work
He is angry that Omar found a mistake
He does not care if the map is accurate
questions.why: Hassan praises Omar's sharp eyes and works with him to fix the harbor, showing he values accurate, careful work.

wrong.A: Hassan listens to and praises Omar.
wrong.C: Hassan is pleased, not angry, about the discovery.
wrong.D: Hassan insists on checking every detail, showing he cares deeply about accuracy.

questions.stem: In the story, to navigate means to —
options: draw a careful picture of a ship
build a brand new harbor by the sea
find a safe way from place to place
copy an old map onto fresh parchment
questions.why: The story explains that sailors depend on the map to navigate, meaning to find their way safely across the sea.

wrong.A: Navigate does not mean drawing a ship.
wrong.B: Navigate does not mean building a harbor.
wrong.D: Copying the map is a separate task from navigating.

questions.stem: Why does Hassan tell Omar to examine every line and label on the map?
options: Because the king enjoys reading long maps in his palace
Because Omar is known as a slow reader at school
Because the parchment used is far too thin for the ink
Because a tiny mistake could send a ship off course
questions.why: Hassan warns Omar that even a small mistake on the map could send a ship toward the wrong shore.

wrong.A: The king's enjoyment of long maps is never mentioned.
wrong.B: The story never calls Omar a slow reader.
wrong.C: The thinness of the parchment is not given as a reason.

MID.prompt: Explain how Omar's careful work helped keep future sailors safe. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how Omar's careful work protected sailors.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Omar's careful work helped keep future sailors safe because he checked his copy line by line against the original map. This careful checking let him notice that the harbor was marked in the wrong place, a mistake that could have sent a ship sailing toward the wrong shore. Because Omar and Master Hassan corrected the harbor's true location before the manuscript left the workshop, any ship later using the map would find the real harbor safely.

keyWords.definition: a document, such as a map or book, written or drawn by hand
keyWords.example: The old manuscript had been copied by hand many centuries ago.

keyWords.definition: to check that something is true or correct
keyWords.example: The scientist asked another lab to verify her results.

keyWords.definition: a person who studies a subject deeply and knows a great deal about it
keyWords.example: The scholar spent years researching ancient trade routes.
The jeweler was meticulous when setting the tiny gemstones.

keyWords.definition: a long journey, especially by sea
keyWords.example: The sailors prepared supplies for their voyage across the ocean.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: Scholars in the twelfth century never disagreed about geography, maps, or the shape of the sea
A meticulous apprentice's verification prevents a dangerous error from reaching sailors
Palermo was the only city with any skilled mapmakers, and no other town in the world had any
Kings in this century had no interest in geography, and they never asked for any maps
questions.why: The story shows how Omar's careful, meticulous checking catches an error that could otherwise have endangered sailors relying on the manuscript.

wrong.A: The story does not discuss disagreement among scholars.
wrong.C: The story never claims Palermo was uniquely skilled.
wrong.D: The king's commission shows strong interest in geography.

questions.stem: Why did the patron commission this particular manuscript?
options: To display the finest geography in his royal library
To replace a ship that had been lost at sea
To settle a dispute between two merchants
To train new apprentices in painting portraits
questions.why: The story states that the king, a powerful patron, commissioned the manuscript to display the finest geography in his royal library.

wrong.B: No lost ship is mentioned in the story.
wrong.C: No dispute between merchants appears in the story.
wrong.D: The manuscript is a map, not a painting lesson.

questions.stem: What does Omar compare his copy against to verify the error?
options: A ship captain's personal logbook from the trip
The king's own private letters to his friends
The original manuscript and earlier notes
A map drawn by a rival geographer
questions.why: The story describes Omar comparing his new copy against the original manuscript and Hassan's earlier notes.

wrong.A: No logbook is mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: The king's letters do not appear in the story.
wrong.D: No rival geographer's map is mentioned.

questions.stem: In the story, meticulous most likely means —
options: careless about every small detail
very careful about small details
extremely fast at finishing work
unwilling to check anything twice
questions.why: Omar's meticulous checking is shown through his slow, careful comparison of every line and label.

wrong.A: Meticulous is the opposite of careless.
wrong.C: The story emphasizes slow, careful work, not speed.
wrong.D: Omar checks the harbor a second time, showing willingness to recheck.

questions.stem: Based on the story, why did the patron's trust depend so heavily on Hassan's reputation?
options: Because the patron himself could not read maps
Because the patron wanted to compete with other kings only
Because Hassan was related to the patron
Because sailors would rely on the manuscript's accuracy
questions.why: The story explains that sailors and merchants would depend on the manuscript to navigate safely, so its accuracy mattered for real, practical reasons.

wrong.A: The story does not say the patron could not read maps.
wrong.B: Competing libraries is not given as the main reason for accuracy.
wrong.C: No family relationship between Hassan and the patron is mentioned.

questions.stem: Which of these events happened first?
options: Omar noticed the harbor did not match the notes
The two mapmakers corrected the harbor's location
The manuscript began its voyage to the king's court
Hassan asked Omar to produce a faithful copy
questions.why: Hassan first asked Omar to copy the manuscript, and only afterward did Omar discover and help correct the harbor error.

wrong.A: Omar's discovery happened after he began copying, not before.
wrong.B: The correction came after the discovery.
wrong.C: The voyage began only after the error had been fixed.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about why Hassan trusted Omar with this task?
options: Omar was related to the patron himself
Hassan had no other apprentices available
Omar had shown patience and care for two years
Omar had sailed on many voyages before
questions.why: The story notes that Omar had spent nearly two years meticulously learning mapmaking, which built the trust Hassan placed in him.

wrong.A: The story never says Omar is related to the patron.
wrong.B: The story does not suggest a lack of other apprentices.
wrong.D: Omar's experience is with mapmaking, not sea travel.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story with Omar's reflection years later?
options: To show that Omar eventually quit mapmaking for a different job
To show that careful work carries real responsibility
To explain exactly how parchment is made from animal skins
To describe a later voyage Omar took himself on a big ship
questions.why: Omar's later reflection connects his careful work directly to the safety of strangers who would depend on the manuscript.

wrong.A: Nothing suggests Omar quit mapmaking.
wrong.C: The story does not describe how parchment is made.
wrong.D: Omar does not take his own sea voyage in the story.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says that small, careful work matters just as much as big, exciting work. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Omar's role in the manuscript's journey.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that small, careful work matters just as much as big, exciting work. Omar's task of copying the manuscript seemed quiet and unglamorous compared to the king's grand commission, yet his meticulous checking caught an error that could have sent real sailors toward the wrong shore. Someone might argue that Master Hassan's overall design mattered more than one apprentice's double-checking, but without Omar's careful verification, even the finest manuscript would have carried a hidden, dangerous mistake on its voyage to the king's court.

options: A teacher
A sailor
A king
A farmer
LOW.why: The text says a king wants the map.

wrong.A: A teacher is not in the story.
wrong.B: A sailor is not named as the one who wants it.
wrong.D: A farmer is not in the story.

LOW.stem: In the story, the word odd means —
options: strange
happy
quick
heavy
LOW.why: Omar sees that the harbor looks wrong, so odd means strange.

wrong.B: Odd does not mean happy.
wrong.C: Odd does not mean quick.
wrong.D: Odd does not mean heavy.

LOW.stem: Why did Omar run to Hassan?
options: He was late for work
He wanted to eat lunch
He had a new idea for a map
He found the harbor wrong
LOW.why: Omar saw that the harbor was in the wrong spot, so he ran to tell Hassan.

wrong.A: Being late is not mentioned.
wrong.B: Lunch is not mentioned.
wrong.C: He found a mistake; he had no new idea.

LOW.stem: What did Hassan and Omar do after Hassan praised Omar's sharp eyes?
options: They sent the map back
They fixed the spot
They drew a new map
They went to see the king
LOW.why: The text says they fix the spot after Hassan says, "Good eyes."

wrong.A: They did not send the map back.
wrong.C: They fixed this map and did not draw a new one.
wrong.D: They fix the map first; only then can it go to the king.

MID.stem: What did Hassan's huge map show?
options: Deserts and mountains only
The sky and the stars
Streets of one small town
Coasts, towns, and rivers
MID.why: The text says the map showed the coastline, towns, rivers, and harbors of many lands.

wrong.A: The map shows more than deserts and mountains.
wrong.B: The sky and stars are not mentioned.
wrong.C: It shows many lands, not one town.

MID.stem: In the story, an apprentice is someone who —
options: learns a skill from an expert
buys maps for the king
sails ships across the sea
sells paper in the market
MID.why: Omar is learning to make maps from Hassan, so he is an apprentice.

wrong.B: The king asked for the map; Omar does not buy maps.
wrong.C: Omar does not sail ships.
wrong.D: Omar does not sell paper.

MID.stem: What made Omar notice the mistake?
options: Hassan told him where to look
His copy did not match the notes
A sailor pointed it out
The ink began to run
MID.why: The harbor on his copy did not match the harbor's true spot in Hassan's old notes.

wrong.A: Hassan was busy and did not point it out.
wrong.C: No sailor is in the story.
wrong.D: Running ink is not mentioned.

MID.stem: Why did Omar hurry to find Hassan before the map was packed?
options: He wanted to leave early
He wanted the king to see it
He wanted to fix it in time
He was afraid of the sea
MID.why: Once the map was packed away the mistake could not be fixed, so he hurried.

wrong.A: Leaving early is not mentioned.
wrong.B: The king should only see a correct map.
wrong.D: Fear of the sea is not mentioned.

HIGH.stem: Where does the story take place?
options: In a desert town in Egypt
In the port city of Palermo
In a mountain village in Persia
On a ship in the Mediterranean
HIGH.why: The text says Omar was learning mapmaking in the port city of Palermo, in Sicily.

wrong.A: Egypt is not named as the setting.
wrong.C: Persia is not named as the setting.
wrong.D: The story happens on land, not on a ship.

HIGH.stem: In the story, a "faithful copy" is one that is —
options: smaller than the original
exactly like the original
much prettier than the original
missing a few small parts
HIGH.why: Omar must check every line so that his copy matches the original exactly.

wrong.A: Size is not the point.
wrong.C: The copy must match the original, not improve it.
wrong.D: A copy missing parts would not be faithful.

HIGH.stem: Why did Hassan tell Omar to examine every symbol with great care?
options: A tiny mistake could mislead a ship
The parchment cost a lot of money
The king liked long maps
Omar was slow at drawing
HIGH.why: Hassan says even the smallest mistake could send a ship toward the wrong shore.

wrong.B: The cost of parchment is not mentioned.
wrong.C: The length of the map is not the reason.
wrong.D: Omar's speed is not the reason.

HIGH.stem: Why does Hassan tell Omar that a mapmaker must verify every detail?
options: To say Omar is not allowed to rest
To warn that sailors may blame Omar
To tell Omar to draw more quickly
To teach why careful checking matters
HIGH.why: His warning about leading sailors into danger teaches Omar why checking each detail matters.

wrong.A: He praises Omar and says nothing about rest.
wrong.B: Blame is not mentioned.
wrong.C: He wants care, not speed.
